summary: Aegis is an offline-first emergency console for astronauts on deep-space missions, built for a tablet. On a Mars transit, a message to the flight surgeon takes around 12-24 minutes each way, so the crew has to act first. A crewmate taps what they see, such as bleeding, chest pain or a burn. Live wearable vitals fill in the rest, and the app ranks the matching procedures from NASA’s own Medical Checklist and opens them with the original pages unmodified. Medications that need surgeon approval are highlighted, with “Contact Surgeon” first. Aegis never diagnoses and never writes drug names or doses. The checklist stays the authority, and the app only finds the right page quickly. The page needs no network at run time. Wearable data is simulated, and the project is a demo, not a medical device.
details:
What it does:

  • A crewmate selects what they see or report. The engine combines that with live vitals and returns ranked checklist procedures, with the top three first.
  • It opens the NASA Medical Checklist (Rev H) pages for those procedures. The app splits the checklist into 68 procedures and highlights the * surgeon-approval medications.
  • It shows live vitals for the whole 4-person crew, with status in words (“Watch”, “Act now”) and the Earth-link delay computed from distance.

How it stays safe:

  • A missing reading is “not measured”, never “normal”, and uncertainty escalates rather than clears.
  • Rate and blood-pressure rules pause during exercise and recovery.
  • Wrist-worn skin temperature never triggers the fever rule.
  • Every rule cites a checklist page.
  • No app-written drug names or doses.

How it works:

  • A simulator streams Garmin watch, Astroskin shirt and glucose patch data to a Flask backend.
  • Triage runs on rolling medians, and across 40 simulated two-hour runs it produced zero false “act now” alerts.
  • The front end is one self-contained HTML page with fonts and photos embedded, so it runs offline.
  • 150 automated tests pass.

Tools: Python, Flask, pypdf/pdfplumber/pypdfium2, HTML/CSS/JavaScript.

Impact: faster, safer first response when help is minutes away, with the crew following NASA’s own procedures.
dataRefs: NASA Medical Checklist, JSC-48031, Generic Rev H (2001)
NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C: Spaceflight Human-System Standard, Crew Health (2023)
